# What breaks first at 10x?

**Rate limit — at 10x the busiest minute needs 35,933 tokens/min against the 8,000 tokens/min ceiling (4.5x over), while cost is only $0.24/day and p95 latency is unchanged at 1.2s.**

The numbers behind the line (all from the 1413-request week of logs):

| | today (1x) | 10x | limit | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| queries / day | 202 | 2,019 | 167/day at 1,198 tok/query (200k TPD) | **12.1x over** (1x is already 1.2x over) |
| busiest minute (11:13 UTC) | 3 queries = 3,593 tok/min | 30 queries = 35,933 tok/min | 8,000 tok/min = 6.7 queries/min | **4.5x over** |
| cost / day | $0.024 | $0.24 | none (no budget set) | fine — $7/month |
| p95 latency | 1.17 s | 1.17 s | no SLO set (sub-5 s assumed) | fine *until* 429s: each 429 retry sleeps and adds seconds |

Why this order: cost scales linearly and tiny ($0.000118/query); latency is per-request and doesn't grow with volume
unless something queues — and the only thing that queues is the rate limiter. This is not hypothetical: I hit the 200k-tokens/day cap
while running this very week's evals (`429 … on tokens per day (TPD): Limit 200000, Used 199123`), which is why the GREEN run is
written to wait out the limit (`eval_week6.py --patient`).

**Caveat on "today":** the week of traffic in `logs/traces.jsonl` is *simulated* (resampled from 32 real traces
at ~220 queries/day) — this demo app has no real users. So the "1x" column is only as real as that assumption; the **ceiling column is
measured** (6.7 queries/min and 167 queries/day at 1,198 tokens/query) and is what you should quote.

First fix (not built this week): move off the free tier / add a second model behind a fallback (LiteLLM router), shrink input
tokens (`MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS` 4000 → 2500 saves ~38% of context tokens), and add prompt caching for the static system prompt.
